blocks.body:
Some configurations become simple once you look at them through the right map of the plane. Two circles tangent at a point are images of each other under a dilation centred there. Two similar triangles sharing a vertex are related by a rotation followed by a scaling. A tangle of circles through one point becomes a set of straight lines after an inversion.

This lesson covers the transformations used in olympiad geometry: isometries, homotheties, spiral similarities and inversion. It relies on angle facts and power of a point from [[circles]].

blocks.title: Isometries
blocks.body:
An isometry is a map of the plane that preserves distances. Every isometry of the plane is a translation, a rotation, a reflection in a line, or a glide reflection (a reflection followed by a translation along the mirror). Composing two reflections is worth knowing: if the mirrors meet at a point $X$ at angle $\theta$, the result is the rotation about $X$ by $2\theta$; if they are parallel at distance $d$, it is a translation by $2d$ perpendicular to them.

Rotations are the natural tool when two equal segments share an endpoint at a known angle, as in squares and equilateral triangles: rotating one onto the other carries a piece of the figure to where it fits with the rest.

blocks.title: Rotating a square
blocks.body: A point $P$ inside the square $ABCD$ satisfies $PA = 1$, $PB = 2$, $PC = 3$. Find $\angle APB$.
blocks.solution:
The three given lengths are scattered; a rotation gathers them into one triangle. Rotate the plane by $90^\circ$ about $B$ in the direction that takes $A$ to $C$, which is possible because $BA = BC$ and $\angle ABC = 90^\circ$. Let $P'$ be the image of $P$. Then $BP' = BP = 2$ and $\angle PBP' = 90^\circ$, so triangle $PBP'$ is an isosceles right triangle with $PP' = 2\sqrt2$ and $\angle BP'P = 45^\circ$. The rotation takes segment $AP$ to segment $CP'$, so $CP' = AP = 1$ and $\angle BP'C = \angle BPA$.

In triangle $PP'C$ we now have $PP'^2 + P'C^2 = 8 + 1 = 9 = PC^2$, so $\angle PP'C = 90^\circ$ by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem. Therefore
$$\angle APB = \angle CP'B = \angle CP'P + \angle PP'B = 90^\circ + 45^\circ = 135^\circ.$$
The addition of angles uses that ray $P'P$ lies inside the angle $CP'B$, which a coordinate check confirms (the square has side $\sqrt{5 + 2\sqrt2} \approx 2.80$).

blocks.title: Homothety
blocks.body:
The homothety with centre $X$ and ratio $k \ne 0$ sends each point $P$ to the point $P'$ with $\overrightarrow{XP'} = k\,\overrightarrow{XP}$. For $k > 0$ the image lies on ray $XP$; for $k < 0$ it lies on the opposite ray, and $k = -1$ is the half-turn about $X$. A homothety maps every line to a parallel line, multiplies all lengths by $|k|$, preserves angles, and maps the circle with centre $Q$ and radius $\rho$ to the circle with centre $Q'$ and radius $|k|\rho$.

Two circles with different radii are related by exactly two homotheties, one of positive and one of negative ratio. Their centres, the external and internal centres of similitude, divide the segment joining the circles' centres externally and internally in the ratio of the radii; external common tangents pass through the first, internal ones through the second. The point of tangency of two tangent circles is a centre of similitude, which is why tangent circles call for homotheties.

blocks.title: The incircle and the excircle
blocks.body: The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$ at $D$, and $D^*$ is the point of the incircle diametrically opposite $D$. The excircle opposite $A$ touches $BC$ at $E$. Prove that $A$, $D^*$, $E$ are collinear and that $BD = CE$.
blocks.solution:
Both circles are tangent to lines $AB$ and $AC$ and lie inside the angle $BAC$, so the homothety $h$ with centre $A$ and ratio $r_a/r > 0$ maps the incircle onto the excircle.

The tangent to the incircle at $D^*$ is parallel to $BC$ (both are perpendicular to $DD^*$), and of the incircle's two tangents parallel to $BC$ it is the one nearer to $A$. A homothety with centre $A$ and positive ratio maps tangents to tangents, keeps their direction, and preserves which of two parallel lines is nearer to $A$. Of the excircle's two tangents parallel to $BC$, the nearer to $A$ is $BC$ itself. So $h$ maps the tangent at $D^*$ to $BC$ and hence maps $D^*$ to the point of contact $E$. Thus $E$ lies on ray $AD^*$.

For the second claim, $BD = s - b$ ([[triangle-centres]]). Let $t$ be the common length of the two tangents from $A$ to the excircle, along lines $AB$ and $AC$. The tangents from $B$ and from $C$ are also equal, so $t = c + BE$ and $t = b + CE$. Adding and using $BE + CE = a$ gives $t = s$, so $CE = s - b = BD$: the points $D$ and $E$ are symmetric about the midpoint of $BC$.

blocks.title: Spiral similarity
blocks.body:
A spiral similarity with centre $X$, angle $	heta$ and ratio $k > 0$ is the rotation about $X$ by $	heta$ followed by the homothety with centre $X$ and ratio $k$. It maps every triangle $XPQ$ to a similar triangle $XP'Q'$ with the same orientation. In coordinates, the rotation by $45^\circ$ about the origin combined with ratio $\sqrt2$ is $(x, y) \mapsto (x - y,\ x + y)$. In complex numbers the spiral similarities other than the identity are exactly the maps $z \mapsto az + b$ with $a 
e 0, 1$ ([[complex-numbers]]).

Given points $A 
e B$ and $C 
e D$ with $\overrightarrow{AB} 
e \overrightarrow{CD}$, there is exactly one spiral similarity taking $A$ to $C$ and $B$ to $D$; when the two vectors are equal, a translation does the job instead. Its centre can be located by a construction with two circles.

blocks.title: Centre of a spiral similarity
blocks.body: Let $A, B, C, D$ be points with $\overrightarrow{AB} \ne \overrightarrow{CD}$, such that lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet at a point $X$ different from all four. If the circles $ABX$ and $CDX$ meet at a second point $S$, then $S$ is the centre of the spiral similarity taking $A$ to $C$ and $B$ to $D$.

It suffices to show that triangles $SAB$ and $SCD$ are similar with the same orientation: then the spiral similarity with centre $S$ that takes $A$ to $C$ (angle $\angle ASC$, ratio $SC/SA$) also takes $B$ to $D$.

To avoid case distinctions, use directed angles $\measuredangle(\ell, m)$ between lines, measured modulo $180^\circ$. In this language, four points $P, Q, U, V$ are concyclic exactly when $\measuredangle(UP, UQ) = \measuredangle(VP, VQ)$, whatever the order of the points on the circle.

Since $S, A, B, X$ are concyclic, $\measuredangle(AS, AB) = \measuredangle(XS, XB)$. Since $X, B, D$ are collinear, $XB$ and $XD$ are the same line; and since $S, C, D, X$ are concyclic, $\measuredangle(XS, XD) = \measuredangle(CS, CD)$. Therefore $\measuredangle(AS, AB) = \measuredangle(CS, CD)$. In the same way, using that $A, C, X$ are collinear,
$$\measuredangle(BS, BA) = \measuredangle(XS, XA) = \measuredangle(XS, XC) = \measuredangle(DS, DC).$$
So two directed angles of triangle $SAB$ equal the corresponding directed angles of triangle $SCD$, and the triangles are similar with the same orientation.

blocks.title: A spiral similarity in coordinates
blocks.body: Find the spiral similarity taking $A = (0,0)$ to $C = (1, 2)$ and $B = (2, 0)$ to $D = (3, 4)$, and check the two-circle construction of its centre.
blocks.solution:
$\overrightarrow{CD} = (2, 2)$ is $\overrightarrow{AB} = (2, 0)$ rotated by $45^\circ$ and scaled by $\sqrt2$, so the map is $f(x, y) = (x - y + 1,\ x + y + 2)$; it sends $A$ to $C$ and $B$ to $(3, 4) = D$. Its centre is its fixed point: $x = x - y + 1$ and $y = x + y + 2$ give $S = (-2, 1)$.

Construction: line $AC$ is $y = 2x$ and line $BD$ is $y = 4x - 8$, meeting at $X = (4, 8)$. The circle $ABX$ is $x^2 + y^2 - 2x - 9y = 0$ and the circle $CDX$ is $x^2 + y^2 + 5x - 15y + 20 = 0$. Both pass through $(-2, 1)$, since $4 + 1 + 4 - 9 = 0$ and $4 + 1 - 10 - 15 + 20 = 0$, so $S$ is their second intersection point.

blocks.title: Inversion
blocks.body:
Let $\omega$ be a circle with centre $O$ and radius $r$. The inversion in $\omega$ maps each point $P \ne O$ to the point $P'$ on ray $OP$ with
$$OP\cdot OP' = r^2.$$
Points inside $\omega$ go outside and vice versa, the points of $\omega$ stay fixed, and inverting twice gives back $P$. The centre $O$ has no image; it is convenient to add a single "point at infinity" and declare that inversion swaps it with $O$.

blocks.title: Inversion of lines and circles

blocks.body:
Distance formula. From $OP\cdot OP' = r^2 = OQ\cdot OQ'$ we get $\frac{OP}{OQ} = \frac{OQ'}{OP'}$. If $O, P, Q$ are not collinear, triangles $OPQ$ and $OQ'P'$ share the angle at $O$, so they are similar (SAS) with ratio $\frac{OQ'}{OP} = \frac{r^2}{OP\cdot OQ}$. This gives the formula, and also $\angle OPQ = \angle OQ'P'$. If $O, P, Q$ are collinear, the formula follows directly from $OP' = r^2/OP$ and $OQ' = r^2/OQ$.

Part 1 is immediate from the definition.

Part 2. Let $\gamma$ be a circle through $O$, let $A$ be the point of $\gamma$ diametrically opposite $O$, and let $A'$ be its image. For any other point $P \ne O$ of $\gamma$, the similarity just proved, with $Q = A$, gives $\angle OA'P' = \angle OPA = 90^\circ$ by Thales. So $P'$ lies on the line $\ell$ through $A'$ perpendicular to $OA$. Conversely, for any point $Y$ of $\ell$ the ray $OY$ meets $\gamma$ at a point $P \ne O$ (the whole of $\ell$ lies on the same side of the tangent at $O$ as $\gamma$), and then $P'$ lies on ray $OY$ and on $\ell$, so $P' = Y$. Thus $\gamma$ without $O$ is mapped onto $\ell$, and since inversion undoes itself, $\ell$ is mapped onto $\gamma$ without $O$. Every line not through $O$ arises in this way: take $A'$ to be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to the line, and $\gamma$ the circle with diameter $OA$.

Part 3. Let $\gamma$ be a circle not through $O$ and let $p \ne 0$ be the power of $O$ with respect to $\gamma$. For $P$ on $\gamma$, let line $OP$ meet $\gamma$ again at $Q$ (with $Q = P$ for a tangent). By the power of a point, $OP\cdot OQ = |p|$, with $Q$ on ray $OP$ if $p > 0$ and on the opposite ray if $p < 0$. Hence $OP' = r^2/OP = \frac{r^2}{|p|}\,OQ$ with $P'$ on ray $OP$; that is, $P'$ is the image of $Q$ under the homothety with centre $O$ and ratio $r^2/p$. As $P$ runs over $\gamma$, so does $Q$, so the image of $\gamma$ is the image of $\gamma$ under this homothety: a circle not through $O$. When $p = r^2$ the ratio is $1$ and $\gamma$ is mapped onto itself.

Inversion also preserves angles between curves (reversing orientation); we omit the proof. Often it is enough that inversion is a bijection away from $O$, so it preserves the number of common points of two curves. Hence two circles tangent at a point $T \ne O$ are mapped to two circles, or a circle and a line, that touch at $T'$, and two circles tangent at $O$ itself become two parallel lines.

blocks.title: Ptolemy by inversion
blocks.body:
Prove Ptolemy's inequality: for any four points $A, B, C, D$ in the plane,
$$AB\cdot CD + AD\cdot BC \ge AC\cdot BD,$$
with equality when $ABCD$ is a convex cyclic quadrilateral.
blocks.solution:
We may assume $B, C, D$ are all different from $A$, since otherwise the inequality is trivial. Invert with centre $A$ and radius $1$, and write $B', C', D'$ for the images. By the distance formula,
$$B'C' = \frac{BC}{AB\cdot AC}, \qquad C'D' = \frac{CD}{AC\cdot AD}, \qquad B'D' = \frac{BD}{AB\cdot AD}.$$
The triangle inequality $B'C' + C'D' \ge B'D'$ becomes, after multiplying by $AB\cdot AC\cdot AD$,
$$BC\cdot AD + CD\cdot AB \ge BD\cdot AC,$$
which is Ptolemy's inequality. Equality holds exactly when $C'$ lies on the segment $B'D'$.

If $ABCD$ is a convex cyclic quadrilateral, its circle passes through the centre of inversion $A$, so it is mapped to a line containing $B'$, $C'$, $D'$. The circle without the point $A$ is mapped continuously and bijectively onto this line, so points keep their order; since $C$ lies on the arc $BD$ not containing $A$, the point $C'$ lies between $B'$ and $D'$. So equality holds, which is Ptolemy's theorem $AC\cdot BD = AB\cdot CD + AD\cdot BC$ for cyclic quadrilaterals. Conversely, equality forces $B'$, $C'$, $D'$ to be collinear with $C'$ in the middle, so $A, B, C, D$ are either concyclic in this order or collinear.

blocks.title: Choosing a transformation
blocks.body:
Rules of thumb: look for a homothety when there are parallel lines or tangent circles; a rotation when equal segments meet at a known angle; a spiral similarity when two similar triangles share a vertex, or two circles meet and lines through their common points appear; inversion when many circles pass through one point or tangencies pile up.

Behind this is Felix Klein's Erlangen programme of 1872: a geometry is the study of the properties of figures invariant under a group of transformations ([[groups]], [[group-actions]]). Euclidean geometry keeps lengths and angles, similarity geometry keeps angles and ratios, and inversive geometry keeps only the family of "circles and lines" and the angles between curves. Choosing a transformation means moving to a simpler picture in which the property you care about is unchanged.

- Inversion does not map the centre of a circle to the centre of the image circle. In part 3 of the theorem the image is a homothetic copy of $\gamma$, and its centre is the homothetic image of the centre of $\gamma$, not the inverse of it.
- A homothety with negative ratio sends the figure through the centre to the other side; check the sign before matching tangents, as in the incircle-excircle example.
- Composing rotations about two different centres gives a rotation about a third centre, or a translation if the angles add up to a multiple of $360^\circ$, not a rotation about either original centre.

Power of a point from [[circles]] is built into inversion: for $P$ outside a circle, the inversion with centre $P$ and radius squared $\operatorname{pow}(P)$ maps that circle onto itself. The homothety with centre $G$ and ratio $-\frac12$ organises the Euler line and nine-point circle of [[triangle-centres]]. In complex coordinates spiral similarities are $z \mapsto az + b$ and inversion in the unit circle is $z \mapsto 1/\bar z$ ([[complex-numbers]], [[analytic-geometry]]); their compositions give the Möbius transformations $z \mapsto \frac{az + b}{cz + d}$ and their conjugates. Rotations about the origin are [[linear-maps]], symmetry groups of figures are [[groups]], and Ptolemy's inequality belongs to [[geo-inequalities]].

1. Show that the composition of two homotheties with different centres and ratios $k_1, k_2$ with $k_1k_2 \ne 1$ is a homothety with ratio $k_1k_2$, and that its centre lies on the line through the two original centres.
2. Under inversion with centre $O$ and radius $r$, what is the image of the circle with centre $O$ and radius $\rho$? What is the image of a circle through $O$ with centre $Q$?
3. Two circles are tangent internally at $T$, and a chord $AB$ of the larger circle touches the smaller circle at $P$. Prove that $TP$ bisects the angle $ATB$.
